traditions.label: Ruthenian Slavonic books and Roman revision
traditions.scope: Eucharistic rubrics and complementary books, with regional reception limits
traditions.coverage_note: Original 1692–1695/1733 terminal comparison, the Univ 1740 bishop's book mandate, Supraśl 1758 and Pochaiv 1788 title and rubric leaves, and 1842/1899 preparation witnesses; later 1905 reprint/1941 rules and dated local reception. Connections beyond those inspected loci are not silently supplied, and books of different presses are not chained by date.

traditions.label: Roman Slavonic Vulgata (Russian-use series)

traditions.coverage_note: Parallel to Ruthenian series; not its successor or derivative. Intended audience is not proof of universal reception.

sources.title: Alphonse Raes, Le Liturgicon ruthène depuis l'Union de Brest, Orientalia Christiana Periodica 8 (1942), pp. 95–143
sources.inspection: Internet Archive volume (Graduate Theological Union copy) located 2026-10-22; title leaf (scan leaf 6) and printed pp. 104–106, 108, 110–121 and 134–143 viewed as page images (scan leaf = printed page + 3); the rest of the article read in the item's text layer only.

sources.title: Sacred Congregation for the Eastern Church, Prot. N. 1219/28, two circulars of 10 September 1941, original Italian text printed in Orientalia Christiana Periodica 8 (1942), pp. 136–143
sources.inspection: Page images of printed pp. 136–138 and 141–142 viewed 2026-10-22; pp. 139–140 and 143 read in the text layer and checked against the images for the cited points. Circular I to the Ruthenian ordinaries is signed by Tisserant and Arata; circular II to the Basilian protoarchimandrite and the rector of the Ruthenian College is signed by Arata for the Cardinal Secretary.
sources.limitations: Published by Raes with the Congregation's permission; the original signed letters were not seen. Circular I says the complete Liturgicon was still in the press on 10 September 1941 and dates the governing plenary decisions to 10 January 1938, approved by Pius XI on 15 January 1938.

sources.title: Служебник … Иоанна Златоустаго, Supraśl 1758, Russian State Library copy in the NEB viewer
sources.inspection: All 181 offered images previously acquired by the byzantine_slavic lane. Re-inspected 2026-10-21: title (image 3), Liturgy leaf 16 recto–verso (images 21–22) and contents (images 176–177). The title describes a Chrysostom Liturgy with services for the Lord's feasts, Marian feasts and principal saints, for the convenience of priests celebrating privately without singing and while travelling. The contents list services for the Holy Eucharist (leaf 76), the Sweet Name of Jesus, the Passion, the Conception, Visitation, Compassion and Rosary of the Mother of God, and, under saints and certain patrons of Poland and Lithuania, Blessed Josaphat, Francis, Dominic, Anthony of Padua, Ignatius Loyola, John Nepomucene and Casimir, followed by votive services.
sources.limitations: Title, one Liturgy opening and contents only; propers texts and the whole Liturgy were not read or collated. The year is read from Cyrillic numerals as catalogued (1758).

stages.label: Basil and Chrysostom in an early Greek euchologion
stages.scope: Identified manuscript contents, not a reconstructed complete medieval rite
stages.witness_label: Vatican, Barberini gr. 336
stages.summary: Basil ff. 1–22v and Chrysostom ff. 23–43v; Basil has a catalogued lacuna.

evidence.claim: Dated s.08(2/2), copied in Calabria; identified Eucharistic sections.

stages.limitations: Copy date does not date composition. No predecessor/successor asserted.
stages.reception: Historical Greek witness; later Catholic reception of this exact text not established.
Roman Greek publication witness; actual use in every Catholic Greek community is not established.
stages.label: Greek Euchologion with prefatory instructions and commemoration condition
stages.scope: Original Greek preliminary instructions, Chrysostom epiclesis approach and intercession
stages.witness_label: Εὐχολόγιον, Rome, Propaganda Fide, 1754
stages.summary: The original Greek preliminaries require papal and Catholic-hierarchy commemoration; the Chrysostom hierarch formula carries a Roman-communion footnote. At the Marian intercession, the printing passes directly to the deacon’s diptychs rubric.

evidence.locus: Title PP7; preliminary PP9–PP10; printed pp. 53–54, PDF pp. 69–70
evidence.claim: Native title, instructions, adjacent intercession items and commemoration footnote directly checked.
The act identifies the four monita; the third includes unction and chrism. The act traces the commemoration provision to a confirmed 1746 decision.
After the ekphonesis Τὰ σὰ ἐκ τῶν σῶν the printing passes directly to the priest's prayer; the Third Hour troparion appears only as incipits inside the deacon's rubric.

stages.limitations: Short Greek excerpts and bounded image comparison only. Papal commemoration and the choir hymn are not asserted to originate in these printing years. No complete predecessor/successor collation.

stages.label: Sinai collection before Demetrius’s additions
stages.scope: Main overtext and identified component liturgies
stages.witness_label: Sinai, Sin. slav. NF 5, with Petersburg fragments BRAN 24.4.8 and RNB glag. 2
stages.summary: Contains Greek-derived Basil, Chrysostom and James material alongside a mixed Apollinaris liturgy.

evidence.claim: Dates overtext and identifies the formerly separated Petersburg portion and mixed contents.

stages.limitations: No direct manuscript collation; source describes a damaged, composite witness.
stages.reception: Sinai collection; no reception into a named modern Catholic recension asserted.

stages.label: Demetrius adds diptych material
stages.scope: Later additions within the same physical collection
stages.witness_label: Sinaitic Liturgiarium: Demetrius’s additions, especially RNB glag. 2
stages.summary: Later diptych includes Western names absent from the relevant main-text passage.

evidence.locus: p. 222, final Textology paragraph; p. 223 and nn. 57–58
evidence.claim: Dates Demetrius’s entries; identifies added diptych and omitted passage at main-part f. 17v.

stages.limitations: Proposed motive for the addition is the scholar’s inference. This is not a new whole-book edition.
stages.reception: Same composite Sinai witness; subsequent use and descent unestablished.

stages.label: Vilnius–Suprasl service book before the appended read-Liturgy order
stages.scope: Original title and terminal rubric state in the NBUV Кир. 5232 copy
stages.witness_label: Sluzhebnik, Vilnius 1692 and Suprasl 1695, NBUV Кир. 5232
stages.summary: The title identifies the 1692 Vilnius component; the book ends with a 1695 Suprasl colophon followed by blank end leaves.

evidence.claim: Original title, copy identity, final colophon and blank leaves directly inspected.
Retrospectively identifies the 1692 codification of Eucharistic rubrics.

stages.limitations: The terminal absence is copy-specific; it does not exclude related rubrics elsewhere in the book or later additions in other copies. No full original text collation.
stages.reception: No universal Ruthenian adoption is inferred from the imprint or this copy.

stages.label: Six-page order for the read Divine Liturgy appended
stages.scope: Distinct appended rubric from after proskomedia through dismissal
stages.witness_label: Univ Sluzhebnik, 1733, three unnumbered leaves after folio 86 verso
stages.summary: After the inherited final services and its own colophon, the book appends a separate order directing the read Liturgy through dismissal.

evidence.claim: Original 1733 Univ colophon and all six appended pages directly inspected.
Attributes the expanded order to Univ 1733 and reports subsequent reprinting.

stages.limitations: The offered scan lacks the printed title and earlier front leaves. The added order is verified as a unit; no claim that every gesture originated in 1733, and no full text collation.
stages.reception: The 1941 circular's regional qualifications remain; print presence alone does not prove uniform observance.

stages.label: Lviv’s eight provisions for private celebration
stages.scope: Private/read-Liturgy provisions, and proskomide and Liturgy rubric revisions applying the 1891 Lviv synod as described by Raes
stages.witness_label: Full Lviv Sluzhebnik, 1905
stages.summary: Eight read-Liturgy provisions are the explicit object of the later circular's corrections; Raes describes the book as applying the liturgical decrees of the 1891 Lviv synod to the proskomide and Liturgy rubrics.

evidence.claim: Identifies full Lviv 1905 Sluzhebnik and its eight provisions.
Identifies the 1905 book as widely used before Roman revision.

evidence.locus: Printed p. 320 = PDF 52; title and reprint statement PDF 1–2
evidence.claim: Later Canadian reprint preserves all eight numbered read-Liturgy provisions, enabling a bounded check against the circular’s account.

The 1905 Liturgicon applies Title V of the 1891 synod: precise preparation rubrics, no angel and cross particle, a shorter formula for the living, only the older Cherubic text, a new Gospel-book rubric, kiss of peace rubrics, omission of the Benedicam psalm, and an eight-point order for the read Liturgy.
Original Italian names the eight points of the 'Messale pieno' of Lviv, 1905.

stages.limitations: Original 1905 impression remains unacquired; the Internet Archive item labelled 1905 (sluzebnik-1905) is byte-identical to the acquired undated Canadian reprint, which lacks opening body pp. 1–272. Only its identified leaves and Raes's description establish readings. No direct descent from Univ 1733 or complete textual identity of every reprint is established.
stages.reception: Institution reports use in Europe and America; extent and uniformity not quantified.

stages.label: Lviv Mikron Leitourgikon under the bishops' 1929 Rome agreement
stages.scope: Title and episcopal blessing leaves, Great Entrance commemoration and epiclesis section of the Chrysostom Liturgy
stages.witness_label: Мікрон Леітоургікон сирѣчь Малый Служебникъ, Lviv 1930
stages.summary: A small Chrysostom Liturgy book issued with the blessing of eleven named bishops who met in Rome in October 1929 and fixed the order and rules of the Liturgy. Its epiclesis passes from the petition sending down the Spirit directly to the blessing of the bread, without the Third Hour troparion, and its Great Entrance commemoration ends with all of us, without Orthodox Christians.

evidence.claim: Title, imprint 1930 and the bishops' blessing referring to the Rome meeting of October 1929.

evidence.locus: Images 34–35 = printed pp. 28–29; image 46 = printed p. 40
evidence.claim: Great Entrance formula and epiclesis read directly.

Describes the 1930 Petit Liturgicon as the text accepted by the bishops at Rome in 1929, its suppression of the troparia before the epiclesis and of the Orthodox Christians wording, and its restoration of the hand-position vignettes.

stages.limitations: Bounded pages; no whole-book collation with 1905 or 1929. Raes's two statements on acceptance conflict (p. 117: not accepted by all bishops; p. 134: approved by all Ruthenian bishops).
stages.reception: Authorized by bishops of Lviv, Stanislaviv, Križevci, Przemyśl, Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, Mukachevo, the Prešov administrator and Canada, with two auxiliaries; actual parish use is not established.

stages.label: Revised Ruthenian Chrysostom book and implementation rules
stages.date_label: Attested by 10 September 1941 circulars; underlying Chrysostom book published 1940
stages.scope: Chrysostom text/rubrics, with separate implementing circulars
stages.witness_label: Sancta et divina Liturgia S. Joannis Chrysostomi, Rome, 1940; circulars I–II, 1941
stages.summary: Pre-epiclesis troparia omitted; private celebration follows common ceremonies with specified accommodations.

evidence.claim: Records omission and other qualified rubrics.
Explains changes from Lviv 1905.

evidence.locus: Circular I, printed pp. 136–139; circular II, pp. 140–143
evidence.claim: Original Italian: the first revised books (a Vespers and Matins extract and the Chrysostom Liturgy in two formats) were sent on 10 September 1941 while the complete Liturgicon was in the press; circular II interprets the eight 1905 points.

stages.limitations: 1941 clarifications are not a separately asserted new printing. Whole book uncollated. The positioned date is the attestation of implementing rules, not a new 1941 printing or the start of universal use.
stages.reception: Circular I preserves territorial rules and older clergy’s private customary use; formation houses directed to new books.

stages.label: Full Ruthenian Liturgikon assembled
stages.scope: Complementary liturgies, daily offices and calendar material
stages.witness_label: Liturgikon, Rome 1942, 678 pages (Raes)

gaps.next_source: Raes (OCP 8, 1942, pp. 104–115) gives page-located descriptions of Univ 1740, Pochaiv 1744 and 1778 and Lviv 1905, and brief characterizations of Pochaiv 1788 and 1791, Przemyśl 1840 and Lviv 1866; check them on the public Internet Archive mirrors of the UGCC commission scans (items sluzebnik_1734, sluzebnik_1778, sluzebnik_1842, sluzebnik_1866; sluzebnik_1798 is the Pochaiv 1788 scan already used, 1692_20250315 holds a Vilnius 1692 Liturgikon, and sluzebnik-1840 is a Chrysostom Liturgy not shown to be the full Przemyśl 1840 Liturgicon). The ordinary Univ 1740/1747 books need NBUV reading-room copies (Кир.5645п, 5646п, 1268) or other holders; Zabolotna's study (https://conference.nbuv.gov.ua/report/view/id/2038) remains the guide to the supplements. The archive.org item labelled 1905 is the known Canadian reprint.
gaps.consequence: 1733, 1740 (bishop's book), 1758, 1788, 1842 and 1899 have original-page evidence at bounded loci, and a scholarly-described 1788→1905 revision is drawn; no continuous descent, first promulgation or uniform reception connects them.

gaps.missing: Original 1905 impression and an original (not photographic) 1940/1942 title leaf; the original signed 1941 circulars; the 1944/1953 Ordo texts; the 1929 Lviv book at the compared loci.
gaps.next_source: The 1941 circulars are now read in their original Italian as printed by Raes, OCP 8 (1942), pp. 136–143 (Internet Archive item orientalia-christiana-periodica_1942_8); the 1942 Liturgikon is read in its 1952 photolithographic reissue (Internet Archive item Sluzebnik1952, colophon p. 678). Still needed: an original 1942 copy (the commission's Drive copy requires sign-in), Museum Bollandianum record 123110 for the 133-page 1944 Ordo, the 1953 Ordo (Google Books records Z5ADGwAACAAJ and HUYCkAEACAAJ have no preview; no Internet Archive copy found by title search 2026-10-22), and the archive.org 1929 Lviv mirror (sluzebnik-1929) at the epiclesis and Great Entrance.
gaps.consequence: Roman corrections of 1941 are primary-described from the original Italian; the 1930 Lviv and Rome 1942 books are compared at two loci. No 1944-to-1953 revision is asserted.

gaps.missing: Exact Russian Synodal exemplar, original 1940/1942 pages, and 1953 added propers.
gaps.next_source: Exact-title Church Slavonic searches for the Roman 1942 and 1953 Sluzhebnik produced bibliographies and the inspected 2021 comparison, but no authenticated public source-book file. The decisive 1953 added propers are identified by that article at second pagination pp. 47–48; the underlying 1940/1942 Russian Synodal exemplar remains unidentified. Internet Archive title searches on 2026-10-22 (Служебникъ, Liturgikon/Leitourgikon/Liturgicon, sluzebnik/služebnik) surfaced only Ruthenian-recension and non-Catholic books, no Russian-use Roman 1940/1942/1953 Sluzhebnik.
gaps.consequence: The intended Russian-use branch and reported calendar addition remain attributed to named sources. Access to the exact original books is the material input needed for independent collation; a failed search is not proof that no accessible copy exists.

gaps.missing: Exact reception and original-language copy identity for jurisdictions beyond the documented Lviv seminary testimony and UGCC norm.
gaps.next_source: Slipyj’s 12 April 1942 Latin letter establishes local use and objections; UGCC decree 4 of 2006 establishes obligation of the named 1953 Ordo. Slovak 1997/2004 and Macedonian 2009 approval notices identify translated services but do not establish their exact original-language source copies. Albanian and Bulgarian official/local-source searches have not authenticated a shared-book adoption act. The 1930 Lviv Mikron Leitourgikon (images 2–4) carries the blessing of bishops of nine jurisdictions in Galicia, Croatia, Transcarpathia, Slovakia, the United States and Canada after their Rome meeting of October 1929; this authorizes one common Chrysostom text but does not prove parish use.
gaps.consequence: Reception is represented at the evidenced local or normative scope; a common recension cannot be assigned to every Church by rite or language alone.
